IYKYK
EYE-why-kay-why-KAY (or spoken in full)
abbreviation (Gen-Z slang)
Abbreviation of if you know, you know, an American phrase for a reference only insiders will catch — an in-joke, a local spot, a shared memory. The full phrase was common in American speech by the 2000s; the initialism spread on Twitter and Instagram in the late 2010s and became a TikTok caption fixture c. 2020, attached to posts deliberately left unexplained.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In current slang iykyk tags something only insiders will understand: a photo of a school hallway, a song from summer camp, a meme with no explanation. Those who get it feel the warm glow of belonging; those who don’t are, by design, left outside. Much of it is harmless — every family has its jokes. The Christian observation: the gospel is the opposite of an in-joke. Christ said, "I spake openly to the world" and "in secret have I said nothing" (Joh 18:20), and He commanded the reverse of a secret: "what ye hear in the ear, that preach ye upon the housetops" (Mat 10:27). There are real mysteries in Scripture, but a Bible mystery is a secret God has now made known, not one hoarded by a clique: "The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever" (Deu 29:29). The early church fought a heresy, Gnosticism, built on exactly the iykyk instinct: salvation by secret knowledge for an enlightened few. Paul answered that in Christ "are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Col 2:3), and that "Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth" (1Co 8:1). The knowledge that saves is open to any sinner who asks: "this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent" (Joh 17:3). A father tells his daughter: enjoy your friends’ jokes, but never make being in the know the prize; and when it comes to Christ, you are the one who explains, to everyone, for free.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen-Z text-speak (phrase 2000s; initialism late 2010s, TikTok c. 2020–present) for "if you know, you know," tagging an insider reference — a harmless in-joke at best, and at worst the clique instinct the gospel overturns by preaching on the housetops.

expand to see more

IYKYK, abbr. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2018–present; Twitter, Instagram, TikTok) "If you know, you know"; marks a reference only insiders will understand. "Third-period lunch table. Iykyk."

Used as a caption left deliberately unexplained; also spoken in full, often with a knowing look. Cousin: "you had to be there."

Older relatives a grandparent will know: the inside joke, the secret handshake, "those who know, know."

Webster (1828), root word know: “KNOW, verb transitive no. preterit tense knew; participle passive known. [&hellip;] 1. To perceive with certainty; to understand clearly; to have a clear and certain perception of truth, fact, or any thing that actually exists. To know a thing pre includes all doubt or uncertainty of its existence.”

Decode for parents: mostly harmless in-jokes; watch for when a phrase like this is used to keep a particular child outside.

Key Scripture

Joh 18:20 — "Jesus answered him, I spake openly to the world; I ever taught in the synagogue, and in the temple, whither the Jews always resort; and in secret have I said nothing."

Mat 10:27 — "What I tell you in darkness, that speak ye in light: and what ye hear in the ear, that preach ye upon the housetops."

Deu 29:29 — "The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law."

1Co 8:1 — "Now as touching things offered unto idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth."

Joh 17:3 — "And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent."

Modern Corruption

IYKYK makes belonging out of what others do not know — the old clique instinct, which the gospel reverses by publishing God’s secret to all.

expand to see more

Every circle has its private language, and a family that laughs at its own old jokes is a good thing. The danger in iykyk is that it turns that pleasure into a sorting tool. The point of the caption is that some will not know, and their not knowing is part of the fun. Schoolyards run on this; so did the ancient mystery cults, whose initiates were sworn to silence, and the Gnostic teachers who troubled the early church with a salvation for those who held the secret. "Knowledge puffeth up" (1Co 8:1) is Paul’s verdict on any knowledge used to stand above a brother.

Christ’s way is the reverse. He taught "openly to the world" (Joh 18:20) and sent His disciples to proclaim from the housetops what He had told them in the ear (Mat 10:27). Even the mysteries of Scripture are mysteries revealed — once hidden, now published to every nation, and "those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever" (Deu 29:29). The Christian who knows the Lord is not an insider guarding a password but a messenger sent to tell everyone. Teach your children to notice the kid who does not get the joke, and to explain the gospel to anyone willing to hear it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English cnawan (to know) → "if you know, you know" (American speech) → iykyk late 2010s → TikTok caption c. 2020.

expand to see more

Old English cnawan — to perceive, recognise, know

Greek gnosis — knowledge; the root of the Gnostic heresy of secret saving knowledge

American speech, 2000s: "if you know, you know" for an insider reference

Late 2010s Twitter and Instagram: initialism iykyk

c. 2020–present: TikTok captions left deliberately unexplained

Usage

""Mrs. Patterson’s substitute plans. Iykyk.""

"What ye hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops (Mat 10:27)."

"Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth (1Co 8:1) — explain the joke to the one left out."
